title: The Fragrant Smoke
subtitle: The villagers burn Putana's body
story:
Putana came to Gokula wearing the shape of a beautiful young woman. She smiled at the cowherd mothers, offered to hold their babies, and seemed as kind as any nurse — but she was a demoness, and she had come to kill the infant Krishna. The child she meant to destroy drew the life out of her instead, and the lovely stranger fell dead at the edge of the village.

Now her true body lay where she had fallen, and no one in Gokula could look at it for long. Released from the pretty form she had worn, she was enormous — so vast that her fall had crushed the trees in a long stretch around her. Her mouth gaped wide, its teeth like the shafts of a plow; her nostrils opened like cave mouths in a mountain; her eyes were deep pits a man might fall into. The cowherds and their wives stood far off, trembling at the sight, and none of them would draw near.

And there, in the middle of all that horror, was the child. Krishna lay on the dead demon's chest, playing as calmly as if he had been set down in his own courtyard on an ordinary morning. The thing that made grown men step back could not trouble him at all.

Then Yasoda, Krishna's mother, came forward, and Rohini with her — the two mothers of the house — and they gathered up the child. The women bathed him, first with cow's urine and then with the fine dust of the cow pen, their way of washing harm away, and sprinkled him with water. Then they passed their hands over his body and chanted over each part of him in turn — his feet, his hands, his waist, his heart, his throat, his head — asking that every limb be guarded. They called on the Lord who holds the discus to stand before him and the Lord who holds the mace behind him, on the bow and the sword to guard his sides, and on the conch to sound above him; on Garuda, the great bird, to watch the ground, and on the Lord of all to stand all around him. And they named every spirit that preys on children and bade them all stay far away.

Meanwhile Nanda and the other cowherds were on the road home from Mathura. They came into the village to find the vast body stretched across the ground and the child safe in the midst of it, and they marveled. Surely, they said to one another, this was no ordinary boy. Surely he was a great sage, or a master of yoga, to have come through such a thing untouched.

Then they took up their axes. They cut the great body to pieces, carried the pieces away, and set them alight.

And here was the strangest thing. The smoke that rose from the fire was not the smoke of burning flesh. It smelled of aloe — sweet and clean and calm — and it drifted up over all of Gokula. The demoness who had come to kill a child had been given a mother's reward, and the air above the fire seemed to say so.
reflection: The fragrant smoke is the story's quiet astonishment. The one who came to destroy a child is granted a mother's reward, and the text marks it not with a lecture but with a sweetness rising from the fire — grace offered even to the one who meant harm.
content_note: The cowherds cut up and burn a demoness's corpse; described with restraint.
next_story_tease: But the danger to the child was not yet over.
hero_scene: The enormous, monstrous body of Putana lies stretched across the ground, and upon its chest the infant Krishna plays unharmed, while cowherds and women watch in awe and terror from a distance.
